newsitem.title: GERMANY: German court fines anti-nuclear activists.
newsitem.headline: German court fines anti-nuclear activists.

text.p: A German court ruled on Friday that 14 anti-nuclear activists had to pay damages for holding up work at a nuclear waste depot in 1990, but the case did not deter other protests across the country.

The regional high court in the northern town of Celle said the amount to be paid still had to be set. A lower court has already ordered the protesters to pay 127,000 marks to the Federal Office for Radiation Protection.
The court ruled that their political opposition to nuclear power did not justify breaking the law, but the protesters could still appeal against the ruling to the Federal Court of Justice.
The court heard that the campaigners occupied two pithead towers for up to six hours, forcing work at the underground nuclear waste depot in Gorleben near Hanover to stop.

The medium-term nuclear depot and planned long-term dump at Gorleben is a favourite target of the anti-nuclear movement and last year more than 19,000 police and border guards were called in to ensure a shipment reached the plant safely.

Police in the nearby city of Magdeburg on Friday broke up a sit-down blockade of 15 anti-nuclear protesters who held up for an hour two rail containers headed for the nuclear waste plant at Morsleben.
The protest follows the sabotage by suspected anti-nuclear demonstrators on Thursday of a stretch of high-speed rail track in southern Germany.

In Bonn, around 20 Greenpeace demonstrators drove a life-size model of a steel nuclear waste container past the Environment Ministry building to protest against a planned shipment of nuclear waste to Gorleben next month.
"The interests of industry are being put before the safety of citizens," said Helmut Hirsch, nuclear expert for Greenpeace environmental group speaking at the demonstration.
Greenpeace said no proper tests had been done to prove that the transport of the nuclear waste would not pose a risk to railway workers, police and inhabitants along the route.
New fears about nuclear shipments were sparked last week when a train carrying nuclear waste through eastern France was derailed, although officials said there was no radiation leak.
